feedback: If a learner says the caterpillar died and a new butterfly appeared, revisit the day-by-day photos of the one named individual and trace the connecting arrows as a single continuous story.
If a learner says the stages could happen in any order, lay their own dated pictures in time order to show the sequence is fixed.
activities.intendedInsight: The caterpillar and the butterfly are the SAME individual changing over time; the stages happen in a fixed order and take real time.
learnerActions: Keep a class caterpillar culture and look at it regularly over several weeks.
Track and name ONE individual caterpillar, recording what it looks like each day with a drawing or photo.
Draw arrows connecting your day-by-day pictures to show it is one creature's story moving through caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly (starting from the egg only if your culture began with eggs).
After the butterfly emerges, say aloud whether it is the same creature you have been watching and how you know.
activities.title: Observe a real class caterpillar culture over weeks

feedback: If a retelling skips the chrysalis or treats it as a pause, ask what is happening to the body inside while we cannot see.

If the drawing shows the caterpillar simply 'growing wings', compare caterpillar and butterfly body parts (legs, mouth, wings) and ask 'where did the extra legs go?' to show a full rebuild, not an add-on.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can reconstruct the ordered transformation themselves and explain it as one creature changing.
learnerActions: After reading a story (e.g. The Very Hungry Caterpillar, which calls the chrysalis a 'cocoon' — real butterflies form a chrysalis, while moths spin cocoons) or watching the real change happen, retell the transformation from caterpillar to butterfly.
Draw the sequence, showing the same creature at each stage.
Answer: is the butterfly the same creature that was the caterpillar, or a new one, and how do you know?
activities.title: Retell or draw the transformation

feedback: If a learner says all baby animals look like small adults, contrast the caterpillar→butterfly rebuild with the grasshopper nymph, which already looks much like a small adult and mostly gets bigger as its wings grow.
Credit answers that reason about whether the body shape is rebuilt, not just whether the animal gets larger.
activities.intendedInsight: A dramatic whole-body change (like caterpillar to butterfly, or tadpole to frog) is different from mostly growing bigger, where the young already looks much like a small adult (like a grasshopper nymph, which has no chrysalis); this distinguishes real understanding from memorised stages.
learnerActions: Consider a grasshopper, which hatches as a nymph that looks like a small grasshopper without working wings, and grows bigger by shedding its skin several times, with its wings developing gradually and no chrysalis.
Consider a tadpole that turns into a frog.
For each, say whether the change is more like the caterpillar's story (a big body rebuild) or more like simple growing bigger, and why.
activities.title: Compare different kinds of change (extension)
